title: Bean tostadas with pico de gallo

notes.text: Warm the beans in two batches, and salt the tomatoes in two colanders so they drain evenly.

move.title: Fine enough to scoop
move.body: Pico de gallo is a fresh salsa of tomato, onion, chile, and cilantro, all cut small enough that every bite on a chip or a tostada gets some of each. Today you'll cut it fine: tomatoes in ¼-inch dice, salted and drained, onion and jalapeño minced, cilantro chopped. It goes on crisp tostada shells over warm mashed pinto beans.

why.title: Small pieces share the bite
why.body: A salsa is eaten in small scoops. If the tomato is in ½-inch chunks and the onion in big pieces, one bite is all tomato and the next is all raw onion. Cut fine, every scoop carries some of each.

why.title: Salt pulls the water out
why.body: Salt on cut tomato draws its juice out through the cut cells. Ten minutes in a colander drains off a few tablespoons of that water, so the pico stays bright and scoopable instead of sitting in a pink puddle that soaks the shell.

why.title: The heat is in the ribs
why.body: Most of a jalapeño's heat is in the white ribs and the seeds around them. Scrape them out for a mild pico, or leave some in for more heat. Wash your hands after, because the oil that makes it hot stays on your fingers.

why.title: Rinse the onion
why.body: Raw onion gets sharper the longer it sits cut. A quick rinse in cold water washes off the juice that stings, so the onion tastes crisp and sweet in the pico.

why.title: Beans as glue
why.body: Mashed beans spread into a layer that holds the toppings on a flat shell. Mashing them with a little of their own liquid keeps them soft enough to spread without cracking the tostada.

wrong.fix: The tomatoes didn't drain long enough. Tip it into the colander for a few minutes, then stir in the cilantro again.
Dice another tomato and stir it in. Next time, scrape out all the ribs and seeds.

wrong.sign: The shell cracks when you spread the beans
wrong.fix: The beans are too stiff. Stir in a spoonful of water and spread gently with the back of a spoon.
Rinse the minced onion in the colander under cold water and pat it dry before it goes in.

quiz.q: Why salt and drain the diced tomatoes?
choices: To pull out their water so the pico isn't soupy
quiz.explain: Salt draws water out of cut cells.

quiz.q: Where is most of a jalapeño's heat?
choices: In the white ribs and seeds
quiz.explain: Scrape them out for a mild pico.

quiz.q: Why cut everything in pico so small?
choices: So every scoop gets some of each
quiz.explain: Big pieces fall off the chip, and one bite is all onion.

quiz.q: What do you do after cutting a jalapeño?
quiz.explain: The oil stays on your fingers and stings your eyes.

steps.text: Set the cutting board on a damp paper towel so it can't slide. Wash the tomatoes, jalapeño, cilantro, and lettuce.

Core the tomatoes and cut each one in half from top to bottom. Lay each half cut side down and cut it into ¼-inch strips, then turn the strips and cut across them at ¼ inch. Put the tomatoes in the colander over the large bowl and toss them with the pico's salt.
steps.look: Even ¼-inch cubes, juice starting to drip into the bowl.

steps.text: While the tomatoes drain, peel the onion half and leave the root on. Cut strips ⅛ inch apart toward the root, then across at ⅛ inch. Put the onion in the small bowl, cover it with cold water for a minute, then drain it and pat it dry.
steps.look: Pieces smaller than a pea, all close to the same size.

steps.text: Cut the jalapeño in half the long way. Scrape out the ribs and seeds with the tip of a spoon. Cut each half into thin strips, then mince them across. Wash your hands with soap right away.
steps.tip: Keep your hands away from your eyes until they're washed.

steps.text: Gather the cilantro into a tight pile and rock the knife through it until it's chopped fine, with no whole leaves.
steps.look: Fine green flecks, not a dark paste.

steps.text: Pour the tomato juice out of the large bowl. Tip the drained tomatoes into the medium bowl and add the onion, jalapeño, cilantro, and lime juice. Stir, then taste it on a piece of lettuce. Add salt a pinch at a time if it needs it.

Open the beans and pour off about half the liquid from each can into the sink. Tip the beans and the rest of their liquid into the large bowl. Mash them with the fork until mostly smooth, with a few whole beans left. Stir in the cumin and the beans' salt.
Cover the bowl with the plate and microwave the beans until steaming, stirring once halfway.
steps.tip: Lift the plate away from you. The steam under it is hot.

steps.text: Stack a few lettuce leaves, roll them up the long way, and slice across the roll into thin ribbons.

Spread about ¼ cup of beans on each tostada shell with the back of the spoon, right to the edge. Top with lettuce, a big spoonful of pico, and the queso fresco. Add sliced avocado and sour cream if you're using them, and eat right away.
steps.look: A layer of beans under everything, so the toppings stay put.
steps.tip: Build each one just before eating, or the shell softens.
